messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 79
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Samuel Adebayo, a seventy-nine-year-old man who had spent most of his life working in a warehouse on the south side of Chicago, had learned to keep moving. He could not afford to stop. Because when he stopped, when the warehouse floor was quiet and the other men had clocked out, something inside him would begin to stir — a feeling so old and so raw that it had no image attached to it, only a sickening drop in his chest, a sudden heat behind his eyes, and a certainty that danger was approaching even when nothing was there.

He was eight years old when he witnessed his father beat his mother. It happened behind their small house in rural Alabama, near a patch of woods where he used to play. That evening he had been out catching fireflies when he heard the shouting. He crept around the side of the house and saw his father’s hand hit his mother’s face, saw her stumble back against the door frame. The screen door slammed shut with a crack that seemed to echo through the ground. His father reeked of cheap whiskey. Samuel stood frozen among the tall grass, the smell of pine and warm earth mixing with the sour alcohol, and he could not move. He did not scream. He did not run for help. He just stood there until his father staggered back inside, and then his mother looked up and saw him, and she put a finger to her lips.

He never told anyone what he saw that night. And over the years the memory itself began to fracture. When he tried to deliberately recall the details — the color of his mother’s dress, the exact words his father shouted — he found only a blur, a blank space where the story should have been. What remained were the pieces: the slam of a door, the smell of whiskey, the feeling of standing in tall grass with his heart in his throat. And the emotion — a wave of helpless terror that could wash over him without warning, without any clear image at all, leaving him disoriented and trembling.

Samuel learned early how to outrun that feeling. He worked double shifts at the warehouse, filling orders and lifting boxes until his arms ached. He made sure he was never alone. He would stay late to help coworkers, take extra breaks in the break room where people were always talking, and after work he would go to the local bar and drink until his mind went soft. The drinking became a nightly ritual — not to remember, but to make sure he did not. The smell of alcohol no longer triggered the memory the way it once had; by now it was just part of his life, the familiar scent of his own glass. But the slam of a door could still stop him cold. At the warehouse, whenever the heavy steel door to the loading dock swung shut with a bang, he would flinch, his hands shaking, and for a split second he would be back in that Alabama yard, unable to move.

The arguments started somewhere in his thirties. He could not say why, but when the old dread crept up on him, he would pick a fight with his wife, with a neighbor, with a coworker who had done nothing wrong. The heat of the argument, the shouting, the rush of adrenaline — it burned away the numbness. He did not realize he was doing it until after, when the damage was done. His wife left him after fifteen years. She told him she could not live with a man who seemed to want to fight someone all the time. Samuel had not disagreed. He understood that he was hard to be around. But he did not know how to stop.

Now, at seventy-nine, he lived alone in a small apartment. He still kept himself in constant motion. He volunteered at a community center just to be around people. He drank beer in the evenings. And the fear had not left him. He could not walk through a park or sit on a bench in a quiet green space; it made his skin crawl, though he could not say why. The woods, the grass, the stillness — it all felt dangerous, as if something terrible was about to happen just out of sight.

What finally brought Samuel to the clinic was a new development. The old blankness in his memory had started to frighten him. He had begun waking in the night, his body flooded with fear, but he could not remember a nightmare — only the feeling, as if his own mind was punishing him for something he could not name. His doctor had referred him after a physical turned up nothing. Samuel came reluctantly. He sat in the chair with his arms crossed and said he did not believe in talking about the past. But there was something in his eyes — a hope, thin and fragile — that maybe, this time, he could finally understand what was chasing him.
